label: lad-cb415
summary: The model's predicted risk is the sigmoid of six ReLU parts added together, with no direct input-to-output edges (the root has 0 of them). Age dominates: risk rises steeply with age, faster for heavier people (age_bmi_rise; switching it off changes the training AUC from 0.937 to 0.866), and women get a lower risk than men up to middle age, a gap that closes with age (young_female_lowering, AUC 0.889 without it). Higher score raises risk, more for rural people, higher income lowers it, more so when the score is low, and more visits raise it, at fewer visits for smokers; insurance has a small effect in both directions, and noise is practically ignored (zeroing its edges changes the AUC from 0.9369 to 0.9368).

leaves.name: age_bmi_rise
leaves.why: Older and heavier people together cross a threshold that raises the predicted risk, and the age-by-bmi probe shows bmi mattering for older people and little for young ones.

leaves.name: young_female_lowering
leaves.why: Women and young people get a lower predicted risk, and the age-by-sex probe shows the female lowering fading with age until it is off for both sexes in old age.

leaves.name: young_uninsured_lowering
leaves.why: The probe confirms what it does (lowers risk for the uninsured below old age and for the young insured), but that has no domain reading and insurance acts in both directions in the whole model.

leaves.name: score_rural_rise
leaves.why: A high score raises the predicted risk, switching on at a lower score for rural than for urban people, as the score-by-urban probe shows.

leaves.name: income_low_score_lowering
leaves.why: Higher income lowers the predicted risk, more when the score is low, as the income-by-score probe shows.

leaves.name: visits_smoker_rise
leaves.why: Several visits raise the predicted risk, with smokers crossing the threshold at fewer visits, and with few visits smoking adds nothing through this part.

overall_function: The network adds six ReLU parts and passes the sum through a sigmoid; there are no direct input-to-output edges. Age is the main driver: the risk is lowered for the young (and for women up to middle age, a sex gap that closes with age) and raised for older people, more steeply when bmi is also high, so age interacts with both sex and bmi through thresholds. Score raises the risk, with a threshold that comes at a lower score for rural than for urban people, while income lowers it, more strongly when the score is low (an income-by-score interaction). Visits raise the risk above a threshold that smoking lowers, so smoking matters mainly for people with several visits; insurance has a small effect in both directions, and the noise input is practically ignored.
